description:
Pluto was found by blinking two photos of the sky. NASA's SPHEREx now photographs the entire sky every six months, and we're building the tool that lets anyone flip through it to catch stars, brown dwarfs and asteroids on the move. 

The data engine already works; now we're making it beautiful and telling its story. Looking for: an astronomy enthusiast, a front-end/design hand, and a storyteller for our demo video.
summary:
SPHEREx Flipbook is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx's all-sky infrared images into a time-lapse anyone can explore. It opens with a journey: scroll from the whole Milky Way down to the Sun's neighbourhood, where the challenge's five targets sit in their true directions at their Gaia DR3 distances. Pick a star and its page shows SPHEREx's six-month passes side by side as a flipbook, a blink comparison and a red/blue difference image, all on one clock, so motion is easy to see.

Behind it, a Python pipeline finds every SPHEREx image covering a position, removes the zodiacal-light glow, masks bad pixels using the mission's quality flags, aligns everything to one north-up grid and stacks each pass.

We built all five targets from 1,142 SPHEREx images and checked each against independent catalogues. Barnard's Star moved 10.18" in a year against Gaia's 10.23"; Epsilon Indi B moved 4.3", under one pixel, against 4.6". Where the data can't support a conclusion, the tool says so: both variable stars saturate SPHEREx, so their brightness change is flagged rather than invented.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- A scroll-driven 3D journey (home page): the Milky Way (an artist's impression, labelled as such) -> the Sun's corner -> our stellar neighbourhood, where the five targets sit in their true directions at Gaia DR3 distances on a logarithmic scale (6 to 2,600 light-years). Each star shows its result; click one to open its page. If a device can't show 3D, a classic page loads instead.

- Each star's page opens in a Compare view: flipbook (every pass in order), blink (first vs last) and difference (red = new or brighter, blue = gone or fainter) side by side on one clock, zoomed onto the target, with the catalogue-predicted position marked. "Focus" opens any view large, with every control: detector (D1–D6, 0.75–5 µm, or all combined), speed, zoom, inverted view.

- A Findings panel: what the object is; "Does it really move / change?" with the measured result vs the catalogue and a noise floor from nearby steady stars; a spectrum (one point per SPHEREx image); and the data provenance.

- Coordinates in decimal or h:m:s / d:m:s, click-to-read coordinates, settings saved in the URL for sharing, works on phones.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find every SPHEREx image covering the position (NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, IRSA).

2. Download small cutouts through IRSA's cutout service, cached, with retries.

3. Subtract the mission's zodiacal-light model and mask bad pixels using the 32-bit quality flags (cosmic rays, overflow, dead or hot pixels, persistence). Saturated star cores are kept for display and marked.

4. Re-project every cutout onto one north-up grid at SPHEREx's native 6.15" pixels.

5. Median-stack each six-month pass per detector; combine the detectors for the "All" view.

6. Measure positions and brightness, compare them with catalogues using nearby steady stars as controls, and export images plus a small data file for the static website.

RESULTS ON ALL FIVE CHALLENGE TARGETS (1,142 SPHEREx images)

- Barnard's Star: moved 10.18" in 0.98 yr; Gaia DR3 predicts 10.23" (0.13 pixel apart); steady stars moved 0.08", so about 123 times the noise.

- Epsilon Indi B: moved 4.31"; catalogue predicts 4.64" (0.05 pixel apart), about 40 times the noise. That is less than one SPHEREx pixel of motion in a year, still caught cleanly.

- WISE 0855-0714 (the coldest known brown dwarf): a tentative detection at 4.4–5 µm. The direction is right, but the measured motion is about 25% short, probably blended with background sources at SPHEREx's depth. Labelled as tentative.

- RW Aurigae and R Draconis (variable stars): both overflow SPHEREx's detectors in 85–100% of images, so brightness ratios are unreliable. The tool flags this instead of reporting false changes. Barnard's Star, which is not variable, shows the same false jumps, which confirms the cause.

Before analysing the data, we wrote down the pass/fail rules, including positive and negative controls.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Volunteers have found most known comets and nearby brown dwarfs by blinking sky images (for example Backyard Worlds with WiseView). SPHEREx adds a new, infrared, all-sky, repeated view. This tool makes it easy for students, amateurs and researchers to use it the same way, and it tells them honestly when the data can't support a conclusion.

TOOLS

Python (Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, NumPy, Matplotlib) for the pipeline; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website (no frameworks); hosted on GitHub Pages. Open source under Apache-2.0.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- One year of SPHEREx data moves even Barnard's Star by only about 1.7 pixels, so Difference mode makes motion obvious.

- Bright stars saturate SPHEREx; the tool decodes the quality flags and says so instead of hiding it.

- Brightness must be compared at matching wavelengths, because SPHEREx's filter colour varies across each detector.

- Areas SPHEREx did not observe in a pass are shown hatched, so they are never mistaken for dark sky.

- On 15 Nov 2026, IRSA's main archive search service (TAP) was down for most of the day. We switched to its backup image search (SIA, Data Release 1) and still built all five targets.

USE OF AI

Code, analysis and webapp were developed with help from Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. All images are real SPHEREx data, and all results were checked against independent catalogues.

RESULTS
Distances: Gaia DR3 parallaxes for Barnard's Star (5.96 ly), Epsilon Indi (11.87 ly), RW Aurigae (509 ly) and R Draconis (2,607 ly); WISE 0855 is too cold for Gaia, so it uses a published infrared parallax.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Spectral Images (DR1/QR3), NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive
WISE / CatWISE2020 catalogue (NASA WISE mission, IRSA)
projectRefs: ESA Gaia Data Release 3 (reference positions and motions)
Gaia DR3 via GAVO Data Center, Heidelberg (mirror used for distances)
